oneSentence: A vector is an ordered list of numbers, and a vector space is a set of same-length vectors that is closed under addition and scaling.
plainExplanation:
In modern language models, many things are turned into vectors: words, parts of words, positions, or intermediate states inside the model. A vector is an ordered list of numbers, such as [0.2, -1.1, 0.7]. Each number can be treated like one coordinate. The whole list acts as one compact description that a computer can compare or transform.

A vector space is the larger set those vectors belong to. It gives the rules for combining them. In a vector space, you can add two vectors and multiply a vector by a number, and the result still stays in the same space. In plain terms, vectors of the same dimension can be combined using consistent operations.

What goes in? Usually text tokens or other inputs are first converted into vectors. What happens next? The model moves those vectors through many calculations, such as comparing, mixing, projecting or otherwise transforming them with matrix operations. A matrix is a table of numbers used to transform one vector into another. What comes out? New vectors that capture useful patterns for the next step, such as attention or prediction.

This is often confused with an embedding. An embedding is one particular kind of vector representation learned so that related items often end up near each other. But not every vector in a transformer is an embedding, and a vector space is not the same thing as one vector. It is also not the same as a physical arrow in school geometry, though that image can help at first.

everydayAnalogy.title: Instructions on a tiled floor
everydayAnalogy.story: Imagine each movement is written as an ordered pair: [3, 2] means three tiles to the right and two forward. Combining [3, 2] with [-1, 4] gives [2, 6], still an ordered pair. Doubling [3, 2] gives [6, 4], also an ordered pair. One instruction is a vector; the set of all such compatible pairs, including fractional and negative movements, is the vector space.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A real noticeboard usually has two visible dimensions, while model vectors often have hundreds or thousands. Also, vectors in a transformer are not manually pinned by people and do not carry fixed human-readable meanings per coordinate. Their numbers are learned and then repeatedly transformed, so the space changes through the network rather than staying like one static board.

visual.title: From token to vector, then through a shared vector space
visual.learningObjective: Show the difference between one vector and the vector space it lives in, and explain how transformers compare and transform vectors during processing.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow diagram. Tokens enter, become vectors, are shown as points inside one labelled vector space, then pass through comparison and transformation stages to produce new vectors. Read it as: input text becomes numeric coordinates, shared space makes them comparable, model operations create updated vectors for the next step.

steps.label: 1. Input token
steps.explanation: Start with a token such as “bank” or “they”. On its own, it is text, not yet usable for model calculations.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a rounded rectangle labelled “token: they” on the left, with a right-pointing arrow.

steps.label: 2. Convert to a vector
steps.explanation: The token is mapped to an ordered list of numbers. That list is one vector.
steps.visualInstruction: Show the token leading to a small card labelled “[0.4, -0.2, 1.1, …]” with a caption “one vector”.

steps.label: 3. Place in a vector space
steps.explanation: The vector belongs to a shared coordinate system where other token vectors also live. That makes comparison and combination possible.
steps.visualInstruction: Place several dots inside a large panel labelled “vector space”; highlight one dot for the current token and a few nearby dots for related tokens.

steps.label: 4. Compare and mix
steps.explanation: The model compares vectors and uses weighted combinations to bring in relevant context from other tokens.
steps.visualInstruction: Add arrows from several dots toward the highlighted dot, with varying line thicknesses to suggest stronger or weaker influence.

steps.label: 5. Output a new vector
steps.explanation: After transformation, the model produces an updated vector that carries contextual information for the next layer or for prediction.
steps.visualInstruction: Show a new vector card on the right labelled “[−0.1, 0.8, 0.3, …]” with a note “updated by context”.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each stage to reveal a short caption and highlight how one token’s vector changes after receiving context from nearby or strongly related vectors.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram is a five-step flow from left to right. First, a token labelled “they” appears as plain text. Second, it is converted into one vector, shown as a list of numbers. Third, that vector is placed inside a large shared area labelled vector space, where several other token vectors appear as nearby or distant points. Fourth, arrows from other points flow toward the selected point, showing that the model compares vectors and mixes information from relevant tokens with different strengths. Fifth, a new list of numbers appears on the right as an updated vector shaped by context. The main lesson is that a vector is one numeric representation, while a vector space is the common system that lets many vectors be compared and transformed.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static five-panel diagram with the same stages: token, one vector, vector space with several points, comparison arrows of different thickness, and an updated vector on the right. No animation; emphasis is shown by colour contrast and labels.

workedExample.scenario: A simplified transformer represents the token “clearance” and its position in a briefing note using three-number vectors. Real systems use many more dimensions, but the arithmetic is the same.
process: Both vectors have three components, so the model can add them component by component: [0.4, -0.2, 0.7] + [0.1, 0.3, -0.1] = [0.5, 0.1, 0.6].
The result is another three-component vector in the same vector space. This illustrates closure under addition.
Suppose attention combines value vectors [1, 0, 2] and [0, 2, -1] with weights 0.25 and 0.75. Scaling gives [0.25, 0, 0.5] and [0, 1.5, -0.75].
Adding the scaled vectors produces [0.25, 1.5, -0.25], again a three-component vector that later layers can process.
workedExample.result: Because addition and scaling preserve the vector length, embeddings, positional information and attention outputs remain compatible with subsequent model operations. The numbers are illustrative and should not be read as named semantic features.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A chief of section in an evaluation office is finalising a handover note for an incoming colleague before close of business. The note records how a proposed search tool represents each paragraph of a cleared evaluation report as a same-length vector, then compares vectors to retrieve passages with similar meaning even when they use different wording.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The vector is the numeric representation of one paragraph. The shared vector space allows the tool to compare, add and transform compatible representations. The same principle underlies token embeddings and hidden states inside a transformer, although those vectors usually have far more dimensions.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Only cleared reports should enter this workflow. Confidential interview notes, personal data and material identifying participants must not be uploaded to a tool that has not been approved for them. Access controls and human review remain necessary, particularly where retrieved passages could be mistaken for evaluation findings.

whyItMatters: If you hear that a model “represents” words or documents numerically, vectors are usually the mechanism. Understanding this helps you ask better questions about similarity, bias, retrieval, clustering and attention. It also helps you separate three different ideas: one vector, the larger vector space, and a learned embedding. For decision-making, this matters because many system behaviours depend on how items are positioned and transformed in that space. Similar-looking items may be grouped together; ambiguous items may shift with context; and errors can come from poor representations, not only from the final output stage. You do not need the full mathematics to recognise what the model is doing and where caution is needed.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A vector is just a direction arrow like in school physics.
commonMisconceptions.correction: That picture can help initially, but in AI a vector is usually treated as an ordered list of numbers in many dimensions, not a literal arrow moving through physical space. The important idea is numeric representation and comparison, not motion.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Vector space means the model stores concepts in neat human-readable dimensions such as gender, place or topic.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Some dimensions may correlate with patterns people can describe, but most coordinates in a learned space do not have a single clear human label. Meaning is usually distributed across many numbers and changes after transformations in each layer.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Vector and embedding mean exactly the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: An embedding is a specific learned vector representation, often used near the input or for retrieval tasks. But transformers also create many other vectors internally, such as queries, keys, values and hidden states. The vector space is the broader coordinate system, not one embedding table.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If two vectors are close, the model has found a true real-world similarity.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Closeness reflects how the system has represented the data for a task, not an objective fact about the world. Similarity can be useful, but it can also reflect training data biases, missing context or design choices.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: A vector is one item written as many numbers. A vector space is the shared numeric landscape where many such items can be compared, combined and moved around by the model.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In transformer systems, tokens and intermediate states are represented as vectors in a high-dimensional vector space, often with dimension d_model. A vector is an element of that space: an ordered numeric array. The space matters because model operations assume closure under addition and scalar multiplication, which allows weighted sums and linear transformations to stay in compatible form. Input embeddings, positional information and hidden states are vectors; matrices project them into new vectors such as queries, keys and values. Attention then compares vectors, often through dot products, and uses the resulting weights to build weighted combinations of value vectors. Distances or angles between vectors can also support similarity measures such as cosine similarity, but those measures depend on the chosen representation and task. In short, a vector is one point or direction in the space; a vector space is the structured set that makes those operations mathematically and computationally consistent.

keyTakeaway: A vector is one ordered numeric representation. A vector space supplies the compatible structure in which models can add, scale, compare and transform such representations.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best distinguishes a vector from a vector space in a transformer?
options: A vector is one list of numbers; a vector space is the shared system that allows many such lists to be compared and combined.
A vector is a text token; a vector space is the model’s final answer.
A vector space is another name for an embedding table, so there is no real difference.
A vector is only used at input, while vector spaces are only used during output.
quickCheck.explanation: A vector is one numeric representation, such as a token’s current state. A vector space is the larger set closed under addition and scaling. Models may compare compatible vectors using dot products. Embeddings are one kind of vector, but not the whole story.

issues.problem: “All such lists” wrongly suggests that numeric lists of any length form one vector space. Vectors in the same numeric vector space must have a compatible fixed dimension, and the set must be closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
issues.fix: A vector is an ordered list of numbers, and a vector space is a set of same-length vectors that is closed under addition and scaling.

issues.problem: The phrase “rotating them through matrix operations” is false. An arbitrary matrix transformation may scale, shear, project or otherwise transform a vector. It is not necessarily a rotation. The explanation also calls a vector space a coordinate system, although a coordinate system is a way to describe vectors rather than the vector space itself.
issues.fix: Replace “rotating them through matrix operations” with “projecting or otherwise transforming them with matrix operations”, and describe the vector space as a set with compatible operations rather than as the coordinate system itself.

issues.problem: The analogy blurs vectors with embeddings and misstates attention. Related items do not become nearby merely because they are vectors in a vector space. Meaningful proximity is a property of a particular learned representation and similarity measure. Attention also does not resolve “they” by checking nearby cards. It uses scores between projected query and key vectors, then combines value vectors.
issues.fix: Replace the proximity claim with “Cards represented by a suitable learned system may appear close under its chosen similarity measure.” Replace the final mapping with “scoring projected word vectors and combining relevant value vectors” mapped to “attention weighting contextual information from other tokens”.

issues.problem: “The space changes through the network” is misleading. The vectors and their representational relationships change between layers, while many layers may still use the same dimensional vector space. Some projections also enter separate query, key or value spaces.
issues.fix: A real noticeboard usually has two visible dimensions, while model vectors often have hundreds or thousands. Also, vectors in a transformer are not manually pinned and do not have fixed human-readable meanings per coordinate. Their values and relationships change through the layers, even when the vector dimension stays fixed. Attention also uses learned projections, not simple visual proximity on one board.

issues.problem: The visual presents token vectors as nearby or distant dots and then draws influence arrows from those dots. This teaches that spatial proximity directly determines attention. Attention normally scores projected query and key vectors and uses the resulting weights to combine value vectors. The visual also attributes comparison to membership in a shared vector space, although a vector space alone provides no similarity measure.
issues.fix: In step 3, show vectors of the same dimension without implying that nearby dots are semantically related. In step 4, show query and key projections producing scores, followed by weighted value vectors forming the update. Make the same change in the description and accessibility text.

issues.problem: The weights sum correctly: 0.18 + 0.05 + 0.41 + 0.07 + 0.22 + 0.07 = 1.00. However, the conclusion does not follow from that arithmetic. A high attention weight to “Lina” in an unspecified head and layer does not by itself prove pronoun resolution or show that the updated vector “aligns” with Lina. No value vectors are supplied, so the claimed weighted vector cannot be computed.
issues.fix: In this simplified illustration, Lina has the largest assumed attention weight for “she”. That may contribute Lina-related information to the update, but one set of attention weights alone does not establish that “she” refers to Lina.

issues.problem: Option 0 is the intended answer, but the three distractors are so plainly absurd that it can be selected without understanding the distinction. Option 1 equates a vector with text and a space with an answer, option 2 denies an explicitly taught distinction, and option 3 invents an input-output restriction. The quiz therefore fails the stated check even though no competing option is defensible.
issues.fix: Keep option 0. Replace the distractors with: “A vector is the whole numeric space; a vector space is one point within it.”, “A vector is any numeric list; a vector space is a learned input embedding.”, and “A vector stores coordinates; a vector space is the matrix that transforms it.”

issues.problem: The explanation lists “comparison” alongside addition and scaling as though comparison were one of the defining vector-space operations. A dot product, distance or similarity measure is additional structure, not guaranteed by the definition of a vector space.
issues.fix: A vector is one numeric representation, such as a token’s current state. A vector space is the larger set closed under addition and scaling. Models may compare compatible vectors using dot products. Embeddings are one kind of vector, but not the whole story.
